timeline.body: The Strait of Hormuz narrows to just 24 miles between Iran and Oman — roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passes through it daily, giving Tehran a chokepoint over the global economy it can threaten without leaving its own waters.

CIA and MI6 overthrew Iran's democratically elected Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh after he nationalized British oil assets, installing Shah Pahlavi as a Western client — the original sin that still poisons every US-Iran negotiation.
Iran's revolution toppled the Shah and established an Islamic republic under Ayatollah Khomeini, turning Washington's closest Gulf ally into its most determined adversary overnight.
Iranian students stormed the US embassy in Tehran and held 52 diplomats hostage for 444 days — Washington imposed sanctions that have never been fully lifted in the four decades since.

Saddam Hussein invaded Iran with tacit US approval, launching an eight-year war that killed half a million people while the US, France, and Gulf states bankrolled Baghdad with weapons, intelligence, and chemical weapons precursors.
Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, and Oman founded the Gulf Cooperation Council, partly as a defensive bloc against Iran's revolutionary calls to overthrow every monarchy in the Gulf.

Israeli jets destroyed Iraq's Osirak nuclear reactor near Baghdad, establishing the Begin Doctrine: Israel would use preemptive military force to prevent any rival in the region from acquiring nuclear weapons.

Iraq began attacking Iranian oil tankers, triggering a four-year Tanker War in which both sides struck over 450 commercial vessels and turned the Strait of Hormuz into the world's most dangerous shipping lane.

The US Navy began reflagging Kuwaiti tankers with American flags and escorting them through the Gulf under Operation Earnest Will — the largest naval convoy operation since World War II and America's first direct military commitment to keeping Hormuz open.
USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air Flight 655 over the Strait of Hormuz, killing all 290 civilians aboard including 66 children — the ship's captain later received a Legion of Merit.

Khomeini accepted the UN ceasefire ending the Iran-Iraq War, comparing it to 'drinking poison' — Iran emerged with its borders intact but a permanent conviction that the international order would never protect it.

Iran sent Washington a secret proposal offering to negotiate on its nuclear program, Hezbollah, Hamas, and recognition of Israel, but the Bush administration — confident after toppling Saddam — refused to reply.

Stuxnet, a cyberweapon built jointly by the US and Israel, destroyed roughly 1,000 Iranian centrifuges at Natanz — the first known cyberattack to cause physical destruction to industrial infrastructure.

Four Iranian nuclear scientists were assassinated in Tehran via car bombs and motorcycle gunmen, widely attributed to Mossad, establishing targeted killing as routine Israeli counter-proliferation policy.

Iran and six world powers signed the JCPOA, trading verified nuclear limits for sanctions relief — the most significant US-Iran diplomatic achievement since the revolution, endorsed unanimously by the UN Security Council.

Trump unilaterally withdrew from the JCPOA despite Iran's verified compliance, reimposing maximum pressure sanctions that cratered Iran's economy and convinced Tehran that American agreements last only until the next election.

Two rounds of explosions damaged six oil tankers near the Strait of Hormuz in May and June, with the US blaming Iran's Revolutionary Guard — the attacks demonstrated how easily a determined actor could shut down Gulf shipping.

A US drone strike killed IRGC Quds Force commander Qasem Soleimani at Baghdad airport — Iran retaliated days later with ballistic missiles against US bases in Iraq, the first direct Iranian military strike on American forces.

Iran launched over 300 drones and missiles directly at Israeli territory for the first time, retaliating for an Israeli strike on its Damascus consulate — decades of shadow war gave way to open state-on-state confrontation.

Iran and Israel fought a 12-day war in June involving direct US military participation on Israel's side, collapsing the last pretense that Washington's role in the conflict was limited to diplomacy and arms sales.

iran-us-israel-war.label: Iran-US-Israel war: Gulf states weigh military entry, Hormuz blockade tightens

timeline.body: President Hayes signed the Posse Comitatus Act barring the federal military from enforcing domestic law — but the civilian agencies Congress would create 124 years later under DHS fall entirely outside its restrictions.

Attorney General Benjamin Civiletti issued two legal opinions establishing that federal agencies must cease operations when their funding lapses, turning congressional budget disputes into government-wide shutdowns for the first time in US history.

President Reagan fired 11,345 striking air traffic controllers and permanently banned them from federal service, establishing the precedent that essential federal workers who keep airports running serve entirely at the government's pleasure.

Speaker Newt Gingrich forced two government shutdowns totaling 26 days after President Clinton vetoed Republican budget proposals, furloughing 800,000 federal workers and normalizing the shutdown as a routine political weapon.

Before 9/11, airport security screening was performed by minimum-wage private contractors hired by airlines — the same system that allowed 19 hijackers to board four commercial flights carrying box cutters on September 11, 2001.

Congress passed the Aviation and Transportation Security Act within 69 days of 9/11, federalizing all airport security screening under the newly created Transportation Security Administration and its 55,000 federal screeners.

The Homeland Security Act merged 22 federal agencies into the Department of Homeland Security, placing TSA, ICE, Border Patrol, the Coast Guard, the Secret Service, and FEMA under a single cabinet secretary with sweeping domestic authority.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement began operations by fusing the enforcement arms of the old Immigration and Naturalization Service and US Customs Service, creating an agency with broader domestic powers than either predecessor and no institutional culture to restrain it.
A 16-day government shutdown over Affordable Care Act funding forced TSA screeners to work without pay as 'essential' employees while 800,000 other federal workers were sent home.

US Customs and Border Protection claims legal authority to stop, question, and search anyone within 100 miles of any US border or coastline — a zone encompassing roughly two-thirds of the American population and every major international airport in the country.

TSA screeners earn a median salary around $47,000 — among the lowest in federal law enforcement — and were excluded from the standard General Schedule federal pay system until a 2023 reclassification that Congress had resisted for two decades.

The longest government shutdown in US history stretched 35 days over border wall funding; TSA sickout rates tripled, security lines exceeded two hours at major hubs, and federal employees lined up at food banks to feed their families.

Congress passed the Government Employee Fair Treatment Act guaranteeing back pay after shutdowns, but the law still permits the government to force essential workers to report for duty indefinitely without a paycheck during the shutdown itself.

The Trump administration rescinded longstanding ICE policies designating courthouses, schools, hospitals, and churches as 'sensitive locations' where immigration enforcement was restricted, expanding operations into spaces previously considered off-limits — including domestic airport terminals.

tsa-ice-dhs-shutdown.label: TSA workers unpaid in second shutdown as ICE militarizes airports
